nameStory: The name 'burbot' comes from the French 'barbotte,' referring to the single whisker-like barbel hanging from its chin. This freshwater member of the cod family has earned many colorful nicknames over the centuries, including 'lawyer' (perhaps because it's bottom-dwelling and hard to get rid of!) and 'eelpout' for its eel-like appearance.
description: The burbot is New England's only freshwater member of the cod family, looking like a cross between an eel and a catfish. This cold-water fish has an elongated, snake-like body covered in small scales and a distinctive single barbel (whisker) under its chin. Burbots can grow quite large, reaching up to 3 feet long, though most caught are smaller. They're mottled brown and yellow with a cream-colored belly, helping them blend into rocky lake and river bottoms.

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Long, eel-like body that feels slippery and muscular to the touch, with a flattened head and tapering tail section

idTips.label: Mouth
idTips.description: Single fleshy barbel (whisker) dangles from the center of the lower jaw like a chin beard - this is the dead giveaway feature

idTips.label: Fins
idTips.description: Two dorsal fins on the back (the second one is very long), with rounded pectoral and pelvic fins that feel soft and fleshy

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Mottled pattern of olive-brown, yellow, and dark brown on top with a pale cream or white belly - looks like camouflaged granite

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Most caught are 12-18 inches, but can grow much larger - they feel surprisingly heavy and solid for their snake-like appearance

idTips.label: Habitat
idTips.description: Found in deep, cold, clear lakes and large rivers, often hiding under rocks or in crevices during the day

habitat: Burbots prefer the deep, cold waters of New England's larger lakes and rivers, especially in northern Vermont, New Hampshire, and Maine. They inhabit areas with rocky or gravelly bottoms where water temperatures stay cool year-round, typically at depths of 20 feet or more. You'll find them in the same waters as lake trout, whitefish, and other cold-water species.

seasonality.spring: Burbots move to deeper waters as temperatures warm and become less active during daylight hours, making them harder to spot from shore.
seasonality.summer: They retreat to the deepest, coldest parts of lakes and rivers, often hiding in rocky crevices and caves during the heat of the day.
seasonality.fall: As water temperatures drop, burbots become more active and start moving toward shallower spawning areas, making this the best time to observe them.
seasonality.winter: This is spawning season under the ice - burbots gather in shallow areas and are most active, often the only time you might see multiple individuals together.

funFact: Burbot are the only fish in North America that spawn under the ice in the dead of winter, writhing together in massive spawning balls that can contain dozens of fish all tangled up like a knot of snakes!
confusionNotes: Young burbots are sometimes mistaken for eels, but eels have no barbel and their dorsal fin starts much farther back on the body. Adult burbots might be confused with large catfish, but catfish have multiple barbels (whiskers) while burbots have just one chin barbel.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'freshwater cod' or 'lawyer,' burbots are often misunderstood as trash fish by anglers, but they're actually prized table fare in many northern countries and are the only truly freshwater member of the cod family worldwide.
compareHints: As the only species in its genus Lota, the burbot stands alone, but it's most similar to its marine cousins like cusk and ling. Unlike these saltwater relatives, the burbot has adapted to freshwater with a more elongated body and different spawning behavior. The single chin barbel and mottled coloration help distinguish it from other members of the cod family.
